# A Defense of Wandering

It began, as so many good things do, with a missed train. I had arrived at the station with twenty minutes to spare, which in the arithmetic of modern life is an awkward amount of time: too long to stand on the platform stamping your feet, too short to start anything meaningful. Everyone else had pulled out their phones. Their thumbs were twitching. Their faces had that particular glow that comes from being nowhere in particular while looking at somewhere else. I did not want to join them. So I did the only thing I could think of: I walked out of the station, crossed the road, and let my feet decide.

I didn't know the neighborhood. I had no map, no destination, no agenda. I simply turned down the first street that looked less busy than the one before it, then took a left because there was a wall covered in ivy, then a right because from a gap in the houses I could see a church spire. This is the glorious thing about wandering: everything is a reason to turn, and nothing is a requirement. A stray cat sitting on a doorstep is as good a compass as any. The smell of baking bread is as valid as a street sign. You are not going anywhere, so you are free to go everywhere.

We have forgotten how to do this. I do not mean the tourist's version of wandering, which is just shopping without a map. I mean the older, stranger practice of walking through the world with no purpose other than to be in it. It sounds easy. It is actually one of the hardest things we can do, because the modern world is the enemy of aimlessness. Every device in your pocket is designed to give you a task. Every app wants you to scroll, to click, to buy, to like, to arrive. The word "efficiency" hangs over our heads like a low ceiling, and under it we spend our days moving in straight lines: from bed to desk, from task to task, from one obligation to the next. We are so good at going from point A to point B that we have forgotten there are points C, D, and E in between, and that sometimes the most valuable thing you can do is take a route that looks completely pointless.

On that walk, I saw a gargoyle above a drainpipe that had been worn smooth by a century of rain. Its mouth was open, as if it were trying to drink the sky. I saw a tiny brown door, no taller than my waist, that probably led to a coal cellar but could have led anywhere. I saw a man in a flannel shirt pruning a rose bush with the tenderness of a surgeon. He was talking to the bush. I heard him say, "There now, old girl, that's the spot." I saw a dust of pollen drifting through an open window and making the sunlight visible. None of this would have been visible from a car. None of it would have survived an Instagram post, because it would have been reduced to a thumbnail, a spectacle, something to consume. But I was not consuming it. I was in it. And that is the first secret of wandering: it turns the world from a sequence of destinations into a texture of encounters.

This is not a new idea. It is older than cities. The philosophers of ancient Greece walked as they taught; the peripatetics got their name from the covered walkways where they paced and argued. Rousseau called his last book *The Reveries of the Solitary Walker*, and spent his final years taking long promenades through the countryside, watching the sun set, listening to the rustling of leaves, and thinking about nothing in particular. Nietzsche said that "only thoughts reached by walking have value," and he walked so much that his family could hardly keep up with him. Darwin built a gravel path, "the Sandwalk," around his house at Down, and walked it every day, kicking a pebble as he passed, and out of these circular ambles came the theory of evolution. Woolf wrote "Street Haunting," an essay in which she goes out to buy a pencil and ends up wandering through London, because, as she says, "the evening may be dark, but it is the dark of the eye which is lit by the imagination." For all of these people, walking was not a break from thinking. It was thinking with the whole body. It was thought made fluid.

And yet somewhere along the way we decided that walking was for exercise. We put on special shoes and tracked our step counts and wore headphones to listen to podcasts while we walked past the world without hearing it. We began to treat the body as a mere vehicle for transporting the brain from one monitor to another. We stopped wandering and started "commuting." The word commute comes from the Latin *commutare*, to change or exchange, and perhaps this is what we are doing: exchanging one kind of life for another, eight hours of ourselves for a paycheck, our attention for a small salary. It is no wonder so many of us feel drained. We spend our days being efficient, and efficiency has a way of squeezing the juice out of everything.

The moment I stepped out of that station, I felt something lighten. It is hard to explain, but when you have no destination, the pressure of time begins to dissolve. You are not late. You are not early. You are just moving. The interval between now and then becomes a fluid that carries you, rather than a deadline that chases you. This is the second secret of wandering: it gives you back the present tense. You cannot wander without being here, because the whole point is to notice what is here. And the more you notice, the more the ordinary world reveals its strangeness. That street light? It is a tiny alien tree. That crack in the pavement? It is a canyon for ants. That woman shouting into her phone? She is a protagonist in a drama you will never understand, and isn't that wonderful.

There is a scientific dimension to this, too. Researchers who study the brain have found that when the mind wanders, it does not go blank; it goes into something called the default mode network, a set of brain regions that become more active when we are not focused on a specific task. This network is associated with self-reflection, memory, imagination, and creativity. It is the reason your best ideas often come when you're in the shower, or washing the dishes, or staring out the window. When you force yourself to focus, you light up the task-positive network. When you let yourself drift, you light up the dreamer inside you. The nineteenth-century scientist Hermann von Helmholtz called it the "three-stage" process of creative insight: saturation, incubation, and illumination. The crucial stage is the middle one, the incubation, during which you are not consciously thinking about the problem at all. You are walking. You are wandering. You are making a mental connection between the sound of rain on a tin roof and the name of a childhood friend. And suddenly, out of nowhere, the answer arrives.

It would be easy to make this sound mystical, but it is really quite practical. The world is full of problems that refuse to be solved by direct assault. You cannot push a creative block out of your way; you have to outflank it. You cannot force yourself to be insightful; you have to trick yourself into it. Wandering is the trick. The eighteenth-century poet William Cowper put it perfectly in a letter: "I never found an idea that was not willing to meet me halfway on a walk." The ideas are there, waiting. They are in the leaves, in the broken glass, in the conversation of strangers at a café. But they will not come to you if you are staring at a spreadsheet. They will come to you if you give yourself enough empty time to meet them.

Of course, the modern world hates empty time. We treat it as a disease. We are afraid of boredom, of silence, of the long blank space on a calendar. So we fill it with noise, with news, with infinite scrolling through images of other people's lives. The machine of the modern attention economy is designed to close every gap, to smooth over every pause, to make sure that at no moment are you alone with your own thoughts. This is not a conspiracy; it's just a business model. Our attention is the commodity, and the machines are efficient. But efficiency is not the same as richness. When you optimize every minute of your day, you cut out the very minutes that make you human.

I remember one afternoon, years ago, sitting on a park bench with no phone. I had been told to wait for a friend who never came. I was stuck for two hours. At first, I was furious. I checked my watch. I counted the pigeons. I rehearsed angry things to say. And then, gradually, I surrendered. I watched the way the clouds changed from gray to pink to purple. I listened to the arguments of two squirrels. I noticed that the man on the next bench was reading a paperback with his lips moving, and I felt a strange tenderness for him. By the time my friend finally texted to say she was sorry, I had forgotten to be angry. I was grateful for the delay. The best part of the day had been the part that didn't go according to plan.

This is what wandering teaches you. It teaches you that plans are not sacred. It teaches you that getting lost is a form of getting found. It teaches you that the shortest distance between two points is a line, but the richest distance is a loop. There is a kind of humility in this. You admit that you do not know what the day will bring. You admit that the world is bigger than your agenda. You let the street lead, and you follow. There is a liberation in that, a lightness. You are no longer the hero of your own story, because you are not even the one holding the pen. The pen is in the hands of the street, the weather, the shape of a building, the sound of a train whistle in the distance.

I think this is part of why wanderers are often moral people. It is hard to hate a place when you have walked its streets. It is hard to dismiss a neighborhood when you have smelled its laundry, heard its children, seen the way its balconies are crammed with flowers. Walking is a form of intimacy. You cannot walk through a place without becoming, in some small way, a part of it. And once you are a part of it, you begin to care. This is the emotional logic behind the old saying that all politics is local. It is why city planners who build pedestrian-friendly streets are doing more than creating convenience; they are creating community. On foot, you meet eyes. You nod to strangers. You ask directions from an old woman, and she tells you about the time she saw a kingfisher in the river, and you stand there in the drizzle, listening, and you realize that you have just become a character in a story that has nothing to do with your own.

But let us not romanticize it too much. Wandering can be hard. It can be cold. There are days when walking is the last thing you want to do, when the fog of sadness sits on your shoulders like a wet coat, and every step seems to announce your own irrelevance. I have had such walks. I have wandered in circles through gray estates, past boarded-up windows, past the smell of chip fat and the sound of barking dogs, and I have felt nothing but a great emptiness. And yet there is something in the act itself, in the rhythm of the feet, in the simple sentence of putting one foot in front of the other, that is like a prayer. You do not have to believe in anything for the prayer to work. You just have to keep going. And somewhere, after the first mile, a strange thing happens: the emptiness begins to fill, not with happiness, but with presence. You are there. You are alive. And for a moment, that is enough.

The urban theorist Jane Jacobs once wrote that "cities have the capability of providing something for everybody, only because, and only when, they are created by everybody." She was talking about sidewalks. She understood that the sidewalk is not just a way to get from one place to another; it is the stage on which the drama of the city is played. The inhabitants of a city are not passive spectators. They are performers, and the sidewalk is their script. The man who waters his plants, the delivery boy who whistles, the two women who sit on a stoop and laugh at a joke you do not hear — these are not obstacles to your commute. They are the reason the city exists. But you will never see them if you are moving too fast, or if you are looking at your phone, or if you are sealed inside a metal box that is moving at fifty kilometers an hour.

There is a kind of grief in this, a grief that many of us carry without knowing it. We have built a world that is hostile to wandering. Suburbs sprawl without sidewalks; office parks are unreachable on foot; roads are wide and fast and loud. The message is clear: walk at your own risk. And so we stay inside. We order our groceries online. We become ghosts in our own neighborhoods. We wonder why we feel disconnected, rootless, lonely. The answer is simple: we have forgotten how to wander. We have traded the meandering path of the foot for the straight line of the car, the train, the click. And in the process, we have lost something that no amount of curated content can replace. We have lost the texture of the everyday.

Perhaps that is why I am writing this. Because I believe that wandering is not a luxury. It is a necessity. It is as fundamental to human health as sleep or music or love. We need moments of not knowing where we are going. We need the luxury of a random turn. We need to be touched by the world, not just in the frictionless way of a screen, but in the full-bodied way of a body. The wind on your neck. The uneven cobblestone under your sole. The smell of rain in the distance. These are not distractions. They are reality. And reality, as anyone who has wandered will tell you, is infinitely more interesting than the feeds we use to escape it.

My missed train left without me. I did not care. I walked for another hour, past a park where dogs were chasing balls, past a café that was closing but let me buy a coffee anyway, past a church whose doors were open and where someone was playing the organ to an empty nave. I went in and sat down. The music was beautiful and sad. I did not know the piece. I did not need to know it. I closed my eyes and let the sound wash over me. When I came out, the day had changed. The light was softer. The air was cooler. The world seemed newly cleared, the way a garden looks after a slow rain.

I eventually found my way back to the station. I waited for the next train, and this time I caught it. But I carried something with me that had not been there that morning. I do not know what to call it. A stillness. A rootedness. A reminder that the map is not the territory, and that the itinerary is not the journey. The poet Wendell Berry has a line: "The impeded stream is the one that sings." We spend so much time trying to clear the obstacles from our lives, to make every stream flow fast and smooth. But perhaps it is the obstacles that make us sing. Perhaps it is the missed trains, the wrong turns, the moments of purposelessness that give our lives their music.

So here is my defense of wandering. It is not an argument for laziness. It is not an excuse to avoid responsibility. It is an insistence that the destination is not the only thing. There is also the route. There is also the stumble. There is also the pause. And in that pause, if we let it, the world can speak to us. Not in grand announcements. Not in profit and loss. But in small, persistent, lowly things: the way a cat crosses a street, the way a door opens, the way a stranger's laugh rises above the traffic and then disappears. These are the moments that make a life worth living. And they are never more than a step away, if we are willing to take a walk without knowing where we are going.

I missed my train that morning. I would do it again. In fact, I think I will. The next train is almost certainly not the one I need. The one I need is the one I have not yet caught, the one that only exists on a route I have not yet chosen. Somewhere out there, a street is waiting. I do not know its name. I do not know what it looks like. But I know that if I wander long enough, I will find it. And that is exactly the point.
